competitors.name: TinyPNG / Tinify (Voormedia)
competitors.model: Freemium, server-side. Free web tool widely reported as 20 images per batch at 5 MB per image; Web Pro reported at $39/yr (raised from $25/yr); Developer API 500 free compressions/month, then $0.009 each to 10,000 and $0.002 above that
competitors.note: The category's default answer and the only consumer brand in it — the panda is the mental model people have for 'compress an image.' Genuinely excellent output (its PNG quantizer beats anything a browser canvas can do) and a clean, ad-free page. Three soft spots. First, everything is uploaded: their own policy is quoted as keeping images for up to 48 hours, which is fatal for anyone compressing a passport scan, a payslip, a client mockup or an NDA'd design. Second, the free cap is per-batch and low, so the exact moment you have a real job — 40 holiday photos — you are asked to pay. Third, the price rose sharply and there is public grumbling about it ('TinyPNG Pro Pricing Is Out of Control' is a live SEO target). Their brand is also being actively parasitised: SERPs for TinyPNG surface tinypngnow.com, tinypng.app and tinypng.blog, none of which are Voormedia.

competitors.name: Squoosh (Google Chrome Labs)
competitors.model: Free, open source (Apache-2.0), no account, fully client-side WebAssembly, installable PWA
competitors.note: The quality benchmark and the closest thing to us architecturally — images never leave the browser, and it ships real codecs (MozJPEG, OxiPNG, WebP, AVIF, JPEG XL) rather than the browser's built-in encoders, so at equal file size it visibly beats a canvas re-encode. Its killer feature is the split-view slider with an independent zoom: you drag the divider across the actual pixels and watch the artefacts appear. The soft spot is enormous and unfixed: no batch. GitHub issue #1259 'Batch / Bulk process' was opened 11 July 2022 and is still open, asking that it 'process ALL images within a designated folder' while preserving EXIF, original filenames and timestamps. It is also codec-nerd UI — encoder names, effort sliders, chroma subsampling — which is exactly wrong for someone whose actual problem is 'the form says maximum 200 KB.' No target-size mode either.

competitors.name: iLoveIMG (Ilovepdf SL)
competitors.model: Freemium, server-side. Premium reported at $4/user/mo billed annually or $7/mo monthly; free tier reported at ~15 files per task, 2,500 credits/month, 200 MB per file for compress/resize/convert
competitors.note: The volume player and the sibling of iLovePDF, so it inherits that brand's search dominance and its business model. Broad toolbelt (compress, resize, crop, convert, watermark, HEIC-to-JPG, bulk rename) and the resize tool takes exact pixel dimensions and percentages, which is genuinely better than our five presets. Soft spots: it uploads everything; the credit meter means a heavy day silently ends your month; the free tier is metered on files-per-task precisely where batch matters; and some free tools stamp a watermark. It is also the archetype of the layout we should not copy — a landing page of red-tinted tool tiles you must choose between before you have even seen your own image.

competitors.name: Bulk Resize Photos (bulkresizephotos.com)
competitors.model: Free, unlimited, no account, client-side (nothing uploaded), monetised by third-party display ads — their privacy policy points at NitroPay
competitors.note: Our single most direct competitor and the one to study hardest, because it already occupies our exact position: browser-only, no upload, no account, no batch limit, ZIP download, plus Chrome/Edge/Firefox extensions, an 11-year-old domain and a 100/100 Scamadviser trust score. Anyone claiming 'no upload' is not differentiated any more; they got there first. The soft spot is the one thing they can never remove: the page is paid for by an ad network, so the ads sit in the workflow, and they are frame-by-frame the same visual signature users are fleeing on the SEO tools. Their framing is also resize-first (percentage / longest side / exact dimensions), which means the byte-count job — 'get under 200 KB' — is left to the user's trial and error.

competitors.name: Adobe Express image resize / compress (free quick actions)
competitors.model: Free tier inside an Adobe account; server-side; reported 40 MB max input; accepts JPEG/PNG/WebP/HEIC
competitors.note: Owns the trust halo — non-technical users type 'Adobe' when they don't know what else to try — and it does accept HEIC, which most free tools do not. Two soft spots that matter. It is an Adobe account funnel: the tool is the front door to a subscription, and the whole surface is designed to move you into the Express editor. And the compressed download is reported to be coerced to a static JPEG regardless of what you put in, so a PNG with transparency or an animated GIF comes back as something else, silently. Also a full upload of the file, on a marketing page with a cookie banner.

competitors.name: ShortPixel
competitors.model: 100 free credits/month; paid from ~$9.99/mo for unlimited; also credit packs. Server-side, WordPress-plugin-first
competitors.note: Strongest at the developer/site-owner end: lossy/glossy/lossless modes, bulk optimisation, WebP and AVIF generation, CDN. Effectively invisible to the person compressing one photo for a form — you have to install a WordPress plugin or make an account to get value. The interesting thing for us is the credit meter: 100/month reads generous until someone runs a media library through it, and the resulting 'out of credits' wall is one of the most cited annoyances in the WordPress optimisation space. Not a competitor for our user, but it sets the price ceiling that makes 'free and unmetered' feel valuable.

competitors.name: Mobile store apps — Compress Photos & Pictures, Image Compress Photo & Video, Photo Compress – Shrink Pics, Compress Photos+, Crunch
competitors.model: Free download, then ads and/or subscription; one-time unlock around $4.99 on some; several are subscription-only
competitors.note: This is where the phone user actually ends up, and where the ugliest evidence lives. Their strength is real: direct camera-roll access and the ability to replace originals in place, which no web app can do. Their soft spots are documented in their own review pages — ads for unrelated apps injected mid-compression, subscription prompts on every option tap, 15-image selection caps, crashes on larger batches, unpredictable quality behaviour, and compressed copies dumped back into the camera roll unlabelled so you cannot tell what was optimised. Several have not been meaningfully updated in years. A web app that opens instantly, has no install, no ad and no cap beats all of them on first impression; it loses only on 'replace the original in my library,' which we should not pretend to solve.

competitors.name: The 'compress to exact KB' SEO swarm — pi7.org, resizeimage.io, mb2kb.com, compresso.io, pixoate, bulkpictools, fast-convert, journaltoolkit and dozens more
competitors.model: Free, ad-monetised, anonymous, frequently AI-generated landing pages, one page per target size
competitors.note: Collectively the biggest thing in the category by traffic, because they are the only ones that answer the query people actually type: 'compress image to 200kb', 'compress jpeg to 50kb', 'resize photo for passport form'. Many now advertise a binary-search quality engine that hits an exact byte target, and many now also claim 'no upload' and 'private.' Their soft spot is provenance: no named company, no About page, ad-dense layouts, near-identical copy across hundreds of domains — precisely the silhouette the FBI Denver field office warned about in March 2025 when it told people to stop using anonymous free file-conversion sites. Our opening is not to out-SEO them; it is to be the one page in that result set that is signed, testable and offline-capable.

competitors.name: Built-in OS tools — macOS Preview 'Adjust Size' / Export quality slider, Windows Photos resize, iOS Shortcuts, and desktop freeware (ImageOptim, Caesium, XnConvert, FileOptimizer)
competitors.model: Free, offline, already installed (or a free download)
competitors.note: The honest baseline, and the reason a lot of technical people never search at all. Preview will batch-resize a whole selection, ImageOptim is a drag-and-drop lossless batch that outperforms any web tool, and XnConvert does 500 formats. The soft spots are discoverability and portability: almost nobody knows Preview can batch, Windows has no equivalent worth using, and none of it exists on the school Chromebook, the work laptop with locked-down installs, or the phone — which is exactly where our user is. Desktop freeware also skews to the person who already knows what a quantizer is; none of it answers 'make this fit 200 KB.'

complaints.complaint: The free tier stops exactly when the job becomes real. TinyPNG's free web tool is reported at 20 images per batch with a 5 MB per-image ceiling — fine for a logo, useless for a folder of phone photos, which is the only reason most people show up.
complaints.source: OMR Reviews TinyPNG pricing page and NitDit's TinyPNG review, both reporting 20 images / 5 MB free. Not confirmed against Voormedia's own pricing page — tinypng.com/pricing 307-redirects to tinify.com/pricing, which returned 404 on fetch.
complaints.weWinIf: No cap of any kind is stated anywhere in the UI, because there isn't one — and the absence is made visible rather than assumed. Raise our own hard limit from 50 (app.js: `if (items.length >= 50)`) to something governed by memory rather than an arbitrary number, and if we must cap, explain why in device terms ('your phone will run out of memory') instead of showing what looks like a paywall.

complaints.complaint: Price escalation on a tool people thought of as free infrastructure. TinyPNG Pro is reported to have gone from $25/yr to $39/yr, generating a whole 'pay once instead' competitor content genre.
complaints.source: onetimesuite.com/blog/shrinkray-tinypng-pro-pricing-is-out-of-control (a competitor's marketing blog — self-serving, but the price figures match OMR's independent listing)
complaints.weWinIf: Put the negative-space list where competitors put a pricing table: no account, no upload, no daily limit, no credit meter, no watermark, no ads, no card on file. Every line answers a specific documented grievance and costs us nothing, because we have no servers to pay for. Add a plain sentence that the tip jar is the only ask and nothing changes if you ignore it.

complaints.complaint: The best-quality client-side tool in the world still cannot do more than one image. Squoosh issue #1259, 'Batch / Bulk process', opened 11 July 2022 and still open: 'it would be great if squoosh.app will be able to process ALL images within a designated folder' — with the processed images saved to an output folder, EXIF preserved, original filenames kept and timestamps retained.
complaints.weWinIf: Batch is already our structural advantage over the one competitor whose output quality beats ours — so make it the visible thing. Drop a folder, see every file, one Compress, one download. And note what that issue actually asks for beyond batch: preserved filenames (we rename to `-small`, which is defensible but should be an option), preserved timestamps and preserved EXIF. All three are currently silently discarded.

complaints.complaint: Ads are injected into the middle of the compression flow, and they are ads for unrelated products. A 2-star App Store review of Compress Photos & Pictures (SmartGundy, 08/04/2024) is entirely about the app showing a promo for an unrelated PDF-scanning app during compression, leaving the reviewer unsure whether the PDF app was required to finish the job.
complaints.source: apps.apple.com/us/app/compress-photos-pictures/id1449007043 review listing, fetched directly (rendered/summarised — treat wording as close paraphrase, the date and star rating are as listed)
complaints.weWinIf: No ad slot, no interstitial, no 'try our other app' — and the studio cross-link stays in the footer colophon where it already is, never in the run/download path. The one place we could get greedy is the moment of success (the toast after Compress); that moment must stay clean, because it is exactly where every competitor monetises.

complaints.complaint: Subscription fatigue on a tool people consider a utility. App Store review of Image Compress Photo & Video (dustoff0499, 06/06/2021): 'I dislike subscription apps... Minus two stars. If I could only purchase the app for a reasonable price I'm in.' A separate 3-star review requests a refund on an auto-renewal after the app stopped working on iOS 16.3.1.
complaints.source: apps.apple.com/us/app/image-compress-photo-video/id1153379683 review listing, fetched directly (same caveat on verbatim wording)
complaints.weWinIf: A tip jar is the only correct monetisation for a utility this small, and it is already wired (CONFIG.tipUrl in app.js). The design job is to make it read as a tip and never as a gate: it must never appear before a result, never disable anything, and never grow or move.

complaints.complaint: Batch selection is capped at absurdly low numbers on phones, and there is no select-all. Feature request on Image Compress Photo & Video (BaldBrain, 05/09/2019): 'let us select more than 15 images at a time, or select all when you're in an album.' iLoveIMG's free web tier is likewise reported at roughly 15 files per task.
complaints.source: apps.apple.com review listing as above; iLoveIMG per-task limit from saasworthy.com/product/iloveimg/pricing and competitor comparison pages — not confirmed on iloveimg.com/pricing itself
complaints.weWinIf: Multi-select is free for us — `<input multiple>` already accepts a whole folder's worth in one dialog. What we lack is the other half: once files are in, there is no way to deselect, remove or clear any of them. Add per-row remove, Clear all, and a select-some model so a 60-photo drop is editable rather than all-or-nothing.

complaints.complaint: Quality controls behave unpredictably, and users cannot form a mental model. 2-star App Store review (redbirdman, 05/16/2019): 'sometimes when you choose 50% the photo comes out 10%, and sometimes visa-versa. And about 1/2 the time just nothing happens.' Separately, the whole 'why does my compressed JPG look blurry' guide genre exists because a percentage means nothing to a non-technical user — the causes named are quality below 50, chroma subsampling, soft resampling and repeated lossy re-saves.
complaints.source: apps.apple.com/us/app/image-compress-photo-video/id1153379683; freetoolonline.com 'Compressed JPG Looks Blurry? Three Causes'; lessmb.com/blog/why-your-compressed-image-looks-blurry-and-how-to-fix-it
complaints.weWinIf: Stop shipping an abstract percentage as the primary control. Our slider says 'Quality: 80%', which is a number about the encoder, not about the outcome. Lead with the outcome — target size, or three named presets whose consequences are stated ('Good for email — about 300 KB, no visible change') — and demote the raw quality slider to an advanced row for people who want it.

complaints.complaint: The output vanishes into the library and you cannot tell what was compressed. 'It needs to have its own folder! So difficult to tell which images were optimized when they are all bunched together' (NoLongerViewer, 10/05/2017); 'all my photos show up extremely small in my camera roll and in reverse order' (badkitty_, 03/28/2019).
complaints.weWinIf: That reverse-order symptom is EXIF date loss — a re-encoded file has no date-taken, so the library files it under 'now' and the album order collapses. We have exactly this bug by construction (canvas re-encode drops all metadata) and we say nothing about it. Fix the naming story (`-small` suffix is good; make it configurable) and give the user an explicit metadata choice with the consequence spelled out: 'Keep the date taken so your photo library still sorts these correctly.'

complaints.complaint: The actual job, for a very large share of this category, is not 'smaller' — it is 'exactly under N kilobytes because a form said so.' There is an entire search economy around 'compress image to 200kb', 'compress jpeg to 50kb', 'compress image to 20kb', driven by passport and visa photo uploads, university admission portals, banking KYC forms and job boards. Tools now advertise binary-search quality engines specifically to hit the number.
complaints.source: SERP cluster for 'compress image to 200kb' — pi7.org, resizeimage.io, mb2kb.com, compresso.io, pixoate.com, bulkpictools.com, fast-convert.com, journaltoolkit.com, webauzar.in 'Government Photo Upload Requirements'. The named portal thresholds (Naukri, passport, visa) come from these tools' own marketing copy and are NOT independently verified; the demand is proven by the page count, not by the specific numbers.
complaints.weWinIf: Ship a target-size mode as a first-class front door, not a hidden option: type or pick a number, we binary-search quality (and, if needed, dimensions) to land just under it, and report the exact result in KB. Offer named presets for the sizes people are actually fighting — 20 KB / 50 KB / 100 KB / 200 KB / 500 KB / 1 MB / 5 MB / 10 MB / 25 MB — and say what each is typically for. Nobody with a real name and no ads currently owns this.

complaints.complaint: HEIC is a dead end everywhere except Safari, and HEIC is the iPhone default. Chrome, Firefox and Edge do not license HEVC and cannot decode HEIC at all; meanwhile government forms, university portals and job applications overwhelmingly accept 'JPG, JPEG, PNG' and nothing else. So the single most common source file in the world cannot be opened by the browser the user is holding.
complaints.source: Multiple 2026 explainers on HEIC browser support (heiccon.com/blog/heic-for-web, photoformatlab.com, fileza.io, convertifyapp.net) all agreeing that only Safari renders HEIC natively; corroborated by Adobe Express listing HEIC as an accepted input, which is a paid-license capability
complaints.weWinIf: VERIFIED GAP: /workspaces/SWS-apps/apps/image-compressor/index.html uses `accept="image/*"`, which happily lets a Windows Chrome user pick .heic; app.js then calls `createImageBitmap(file)`, throws, and toasts 'Couldn't read <name>.' That is the worst possible ending. Detect the extension before decoding and give a real answer: name the format, explain that this browser has no HEIC decoder, and offer the two routes out — open in Safari, or iPhone Settings → Camera → Formats → Most Compatible. If we ever want to actually solve it, a lazily-loaded WASM HEIC decoder is the single highest-value addition to this app.

complaints.complaint: Browser canvas re-encoding routinely makes PNGs BIGGER than the input. A documented case: an image under 8 MB on disk came out over 29 MB after a canvas round-trip. MDN is explicit that if no format is given the output is PNG, and PNG from canvas is unquantised lossless RGBA — so a screenshot or a flat-colour graphic re-encoded through canvas inflates.
complaints.source: github.com/fengyuanchen/cropper/issues/542 'Large images have their file size dramatically increased'; MDN HTMLCanvasElement.toBlob / toDataURL documentation
complaints.weWinIf: VERIFIED GAP: in app.js, `compressOne` calls `canvasToBlob(canvas, type, format === 'png' ? undefined : quality)` with no quantizer, and `savingsPct()` in helpers.js returns 0 whenever after >= before. So a user who picks PNG can be handed a file several times larger, the row will show the new bigger size with no warning, and the Save button still offers it. Hard rule: never return a file larger than the input. Fall back to the original bytes, say so plainly ('PNG re-encode would make this 3× bigger — kept your original'), and suggest WebP, which is the correct answer for graphics anyway.

complaints.complaint: Colours come back duller than the original on modern phones. A 2D canvas created without an explicit colorSpace is limited to sRGB and clips everything outside that gamut, and iPhones shoot Display P3 by default. Chrome has supported Display-P3 canvas since 111 and Safari since 15.1, so the fix exists and is not being applied.
complaints.source: WICG canvas-color-space explainer (Canvas2DColorManagementExplainer.md); WebKit blog 'Wide Gamut 2D Graphics using HTML Canvas'; MDN ImageData.colorSpace
complaints.weWinIf: VERIFIED GAP: app.js calls `canvas.getContext('2d')` with no options, so every wide-gamut photo we touch is silently gamut-clipped — saturated reds, sunsets, foliage and neon lose their punch, and the user blames 'compression.' Request `{ colorSpace: 'display-p3' }` with a feature-detect fallback, and then say it: 'colours are preserved, not flattened to sRGB' is a claim no free competitor makes and one that a photographer will immediately test.

complaints.complaint: 'Free online image tool' is now a security signal, not a convenience one. In March 2025 the FBI Denver field office publicly warned that free online file-converter sites are being used to deliver malware — ransomware, infostealers, browser hijackers — and that criminals buy search ads to put those sites at the top of results for 'free online file converter.' The image-compression SERP is the same shape: hundreds of near-identical anonymous domains, plus outright brand parasites around TinyPNG (tinypngnow.com, tinypng.app, tinypng.blog).
complaints.source: fbi.gov/contact-us/field-offices/denver/news/fbi-denver-warns-of-online-file-converter-scam, reported independently by Malwarebytes, BleepingComputer, Help Net Security, Bitdefender and Forbes (18 March 2025). Clone domains observed directly in search results for TinyPNG queries.
complaints.weWinIf: Being generic is now a liability. Sign the page: a real studio name, a real About and privacy page, a real feedback address (we have one in the colophon), a visible link to the source, and — the thing nobody else can offer — an explicit invitation to falsify the claim: 'Turn off your Wi-Fi. It still works.' We already precache everything in sw.js, so this is true today and merely unsaid.

complaints.complaint: 'Private, no upload, in your browser' is no longer a differentiator — it is a crowded marketing claim. A single search returns a dozen competing pages all asserting it (imagera.ai, webtoolverse, pickrack, imagepal, wildandfreetools, orthogonal.info, minipx, fastcompressor, compresso.io), and bulkresizephotos.com has been doing it genuinely for eleven years with a 100/100 trust score and browser extensions.
complaints.source: SERP for 'TinyPNG alternative no upload' — every result on page one is a competing tool marketing its own privacy. These are self-serving sources and none of their numbers should be quoted; the finding is the shape of the page, not its content.
complaints.weWinIf: Assume the claim is discounted on arrival and compete one level up: make it *testable* (offline PWA, airplane-mode challenge), make it *attributable* (named LLC, named human, feedback email), and make it *structural* (a strict same-origin CSP, no analytics, no fonts from a CDN — all of which the build already satisfies). Then win on the things a page paid for by ads cannot copy: no ad slot, no cookie banner, and a genuinely better-looking tool.

tableStakes: Drag and drop files or a whole folder onto the page, plus paste from clipboard (Cmd/Ctrl-V of a screenshot). VERIFIED GAP IN OUR BUILD: /workspaces/SWS-apps/apps/image-compressor/index.html offers only a '🖼️ Choose images' button driving a hidden `<input type="file" accept="image/*" multiple>`; app.js registers no dragover, drop or paste handler anywhere. Every competitor in the category — TinyPNG, Squoosh, iLoveIMG, bulkresizephotos — leads with a dropzone, and screenshot-paste is the fastest path for the web-worker use case.

Download everything as a single ZIP. VERIFIED GAP: app.js `downloadStaggered()` fires N separate `<a download>` clicks 350 ms apart and shows the toast 'If the browser asks about multiple downloads, allow it' — i.e. we ask the user to grant a permission that reads like an attack. Chrome throws a multiple-downloads permission bar; Safari is documented to drop queued files rather than download them, so a 30-photo batch on an iPad largely fails. A ZIP is the category norm and requires one small vendored zip writer.

A real before/after preview of the OUTPUT at 1:1, not just numbers. VERIFIED GAP: `render()` in app.js shows a 120 px JPEG-quality-0.7 thumbnail of the ORIGINAL plus text byte counts; the compressed result is never displayed. The user downloads a file they have never seen. Squoosh's split-view slider is the reason people trust it, and the single most-cited fear in this category is 'will it look bad.'

Compress to a target file size. VERIFIED GAP: our only controls are a 30–95 `<input type="range" id="quality">` and a five-option `<select id="maxSide">`. A whole tier of the market exists solely to serve 'get this under 200 KB', and hitting it by dragging a quality slider and re-running is exactly the loop those tools remove.

Remove one image, and clear the list. VERIFIED GAP: `render()` emits a thumbnail, a text row and a per-item 'Save' button — there is no per-row delete, no Clear all, and no way to deselect. Once 50 files are in (`if (items.length >= 50)`), the only exit is reloading the page, which throws away every compressed result.

Accept HEIC. VERIFIED GAP: `accept="image/*"` lets the file picker offer .heic on Windows and Android, `createImageBitmap` then throws in every non-Safari browser, and the user gets 'Couldn't read IMG_4821.HEIC' with no explanation and no route out. Adobe Express and iLoveIMG both accept HEIC; it is the iPhone default format and therefore a large share of every real batch.

Exact output dimensions and percentage scaling, not just presets. VERIFIED GAP: `<select id="maxSide">` offers 3000 / 1920 / 1280 / 800 / keep, and nothing else. iLoveIMG and bulkresizephotos both take a typed width × height with aspect lock, and percentage. Forms that specify pixel dimensions (passport 600×600, avatar 400×400) cannot be served at all by our current control.

Visible per-file progress with a working cancel, and work moved off the main thread. VERIFIED GAP: the Compress handler sets `btn.textContent = 'Working…'`, disables the button, and runs a serial `for` loop of `createImageBitmap` + `drawImage` + `toBlob` on the main thread. Fifty 12-megapixel photos will lock the tab for tens of seconds with no progress and no way to stop. A Web Worker with OffscreenCanvas fixes both.

AVIF output. VERIFIED GAP: `<select id="format">` offers jpeg / webp / png only. Chrome 124+ can encode AVIF via `canvas.toBlob('image/avif')`; Firefox and Safari cannot, so it must be feature-detected — but Squoosh, ShortPixel and the newer web tools all offer it and it is 20–30% smaller than WebP at equal quality.

An explicit, stated metadata policy in both directions. VERIFIED GAP: a canvas re-encode silently drops all EXIF, IPTC and ICC data — including GPS coordinates (a privacy win we never claim) and date-taken (a loss that scrambles the user's photo library, and which shows up verbatim in competitor reviews as 'in reverse order'). Nothing in index.html, app.js or the footer colophon mentions metadata at all.

The privacy promise stated as an object, not as body copy. VERIFIED GAP: index.html defines a `.trust` component in CSS (5 references, including a print override) but never uses it — `grep 'class="trust' index.html` returns nothing. The promise currently lives in a hero paragraph and the footer colophon, which is exactly the grey-body-copy form the cross-portfolio brief says users do not believe.

Never return a file bigger than the one you were given. VERIFIED GAP: the PNG path calls `toBlob` with `undefined` quality and no quantizer, canvas PNG is well documented to inflate, and `savingsPct()` returns 0 rather than a negative — so an inflated result is displayed as a neutral '→ 29.4 MB' with a live Save button. A tool that can silently hand back a worse file than it received has failed at its one job.
differentiators: Own the byte target. Make 'fit it under ___' the primary control and the raw quality slider the advanced one: type a number or pick from presets tied to the caps people actually hit (200 KB form uploads, 20/50 KB signature fields, 10 MB Discord, 25 MB Gmail attachment), binary-search quality and, if necessary, dimensions, and report the exact landed size. The entire 'compress to 200kb' economy is anonymous ad-funded pages; nobody with a name, no ads and an offline PWA is competing for that job.

Make the privacy claim falsifiable rather than asserted. Everyone now says 'no upload' — bulkresizephotos has said it for eleven years, and a dozen SEO clones say it too. What none of them can offer is a five-second test: 'turn off your Wi-Fi; it still works.' sw.js already precaches the whole app, so this is true today and merely unstated. Pair it with the negative-space list (no account, no cap, no credits, no watermark, no ads, no card) placed exactly where competitors put a pricing table.

An explicit metadata switch with the consequences written out. 'Remove location and camera info (recommended)' answers the reason people avoid uploading photos at all; 'Keep the date taken so your photo library sorts these correctly' answers the real, reviewed complaint that compressed copies land in the camera roll in the wrong order. Every competitor either strips silently or preserves silently; naming it turns a hidden defect into the most trustworthy thing on the page.

Photographic-neutral chrome and an honest 1:1 comparison. This is the only app in the portfolio whose subject matter is colour fidelity, and it is currently wrapped in a saturated magenta wash — you cannot judge whether a photo shifted when the surround is pink. Put every preview on a fixed neutral grey field that does not change with the theme, give a draggable before/after divider with pixel-level zoom, and pre-position the divider on the region most likely to show artefacts (edges, text, sky gradients). Squoosh proves people trust the tool that shows them the damage.

Colour-managed output, and say so. Request `getContext('2d', { colorSpace: 'display-p3' })` with a feature-detect fallback so iPhone photos do not come back gamut-clipped and dull. 'We don't flatten your colours' is a claim no free competitor makes, and it is instantly testable by exactly the sceptical user we most want.

A hard promise never to make a file worse. If a re-encode would inflate the file, hand back the original bytes and say why in one plain sentence, with the better option offered ('this is a flat graphic — WebP will be 70% smaller than PNG'). Turning the category's most common silent failure into a visible piece of honesty is cheap and memorable.

Meet the phone where it is: add `share_target` to manifest.webmanifest so an installed Android PWA appears in the system share sheet and photos can be sent straight from the gallery, and `file_handlers` on desktop so double-clicking a JPEG can open it here. Zero free competitors do this, it removes the entire file-picker step, and it is a manifest change rather than a rewrite.

Failure messages that are actually a route out. HEIC, RAW, CMYK TIFFs, SVGs and 200 MB panoramas will all arrive. Name the format, explain in one line why this browser cannot decode it, and give the concrete next step (open in Safari; iPhone Settings → Camera → Formats → Most Compatible). 'Couldn't read IMG_4821.HEIC' is the current message and it is the app's worst moment.

Remember the recipe without an account. Store the last target size, format and metadata choice in localStorage — the same person is compressing the same kind of thing for the same portal every month. Personalisation with no login is the one thing an account-based competitor structurally cannot match.

aesthetic.categoryConventions: Three visual dialects, all of them beatable. (1) The mascot-friendly consumer tool: TinyPNG's panda, rounded illustration, big pastel dropzone, everything soft — warm and trustworthy, but it reads as a 2015 startup and it is being cloned by parasite domains that copy the look exactly. (2) The tool-grid portal: iLoveIMG (and Adobe Express) — a marketing landing page first, then a wall of coloured tiles you must choose between before you have even seen your image, plus a cookie banner, an ad rail and a 'trusted by N million' badge. (3) The codec-nerd instrument: Squoosh — dark, technical, encoder names and effort sliders exposed, a split-view comparison that is genuinely the best idea in the category, wrapped in a bright multicolour gradient that fights the images it is showing. Underneath all three sits the SEO swarm, whose house style is a giant dashed rectangle occupying the whole viewport, an H1 that is literally the search query ('Compress Image to 200KB'), a tick-mark feature table, and two ad units. Dated tells in 2026: skeuomorphic stacked-photo illustrations, rainbow gradient heroes, percentage-saved counters that animate up with confetti, oversized dashed dropzones, glassmorphic cards, mascots, and any interstitial between 'done' and 'download'. What reads as current: the working surface visible with zero scroll and no landing preamble; near-neutral instrument chrome so the images are the only saturated thing on screen; exactly one accent used for state rather than decoration; large, exact, monospaced-feeling numbers (KB, pixel dimensions, percentages) treated as the typography of the page; real dark mode rather than an inverted afterthought; and results shown as pictures, not as a table of byte counts. Because the SERP is full of anonymous near-identical clones and the FBI has publicly warned about that exact silhouette, looking generic is now an active liability — visual specificity is a trust signal, not a vanity one.
aesthetic.emotionalContext: Three distinct people arrive here, all of them blocked rather than curious. The largest group by volume is the form-filler: someone whose passport application, visa portal, university admission page, bank KYC upload or job-board profile has just rejected their photo with 'maximum 200 KB'. They are often on an Android phone, frequently not a native English speaker, often photographing a printed document under bad light, and they do not know or care what a quality percentage is — they know one number and they need to be under it. Their deadline is usually a session timeout. The second group is the sender: someone with 40 holiday photos that won't attach to an email, or twelve listing photos for Marketplace/eBay/Etsy, on a laptop, mildly irritated, wanting the whole batch done in one gesture and put somewhere they can find it. The third is the maker — the person shrinking assets for a site or a deck — who is the most sceptical about quality and the most likely to test us against Squoosh. What all three share is a specific fear that is not privacy: it is 'this is going to look bad and I won't notice until it's too late.' Privacy is the reason they choose us; visible quality is the reason they come back. That dictates: the drop surface and the result both above the fold with no scroll; the output shown as an image, not a number, before it is downloaded; file sizes rendered large and exact in KB/MB, never as vague words; a single unambiguous primary action per screen; 44 px+ targets and nothing that moves in the thumb zone, because the phone user is one-handed; body text no smaller than 16 px; and absolutely no celebratory animation on completion — the moment of success is the moment they want to leave, and every millisecond of delight is a tax on someone who is already late. The register is a good workshop instrument: calm, exact, self-effacing, and completely uninterested in your attention.
aesthetic.recommendedFeel: instrument-neutral, exact, quiet, fast, honest, unfussy

colorRecommendation.hueFamily: A cool photographic graphite shell — near-achromatic neutrals (chroma ≈ 0.010–0.020) carried on a faint violet axis around hue 316–320 so the greys still belong to this app's row in the studio — with ONE high-chroma magenta-violet at hue ≈ 318, chroma ≈ 0.16, reserved for the primary action and the savings figure. Crucially, add a fixed, theme-independent mid-grey viewing field (L ≈ 0.55, chroma 0) behind every image preview. Keep the existing green support hue (158) for 'smaller', but never let it be the only signal. Drop the `wash` texture to `none`, and use a real alpha checkerboard only where transparency actually exists.
colorRecommendation.rationale: Four forces, and the functional one is decisive. (1) FUNCTION. This is the only app in the portfolio whose subject matter is colour fidelity. The user's job is to look at a photo and decide whether compression hurt it, and simultaneous contrast means a saturated surround makes that judgement impossible — a pink wash behind a thumbnail pushes greens and skin tones perceptually the wrong way. Every serious tool that asks a human to judge an image (Lightroom, Photoshop, Capture One, Preview, Squoosh) uses near-neutral chrome and a neutral field behind the image, and they do it for this exact reason. Our current skin is the opposite: hue 322 at chroma 0.145 with `texture: 'wash'`, i.e. two radial colour washes painted behind the content, plus `--accent:#8e479a` on a `#fcf5fd` pink-white canvas per manifest.webmanifest and the theme-color metas. That is the single most consequential mistake in the current build, because it degrades the one perceptual task the app exists to support. (2) PORTFOLIO. Read /workspaces/SWS-apps/design/skins.mjs: the 276–350 arc is the most crowded stretch of the wheel — pdf-tools 276, baby-log 294, seating-chart 310, image-compressor 322, wedding-timeline 336, wheel-picker 350, with secret-santa at 8 just past it. Six apps in 74°. skins.mjs itself concedes hue uniqueness is gone at 23 apps and says to push apps apart on the other four axes. This recommendation does exactly that without moving hue at all, which also preserves the hub rule (image-compressor stays far from its Paper & Files siblings qr-maker 142, scan-to-pdf 202, signature-maker 264, pdf-tools 276). Against wedding-timeline (336) and seating-chart (310): those are warm cream, editorial voice, wash texture, light pages — ours becomes cool graphite, technical voice, no texture, mid-dark. Temperature and value alone separate them at a glance. Against wheel-picker (350, cool, chroma 0.175, r 22): wheel-picker is the deliberately loud one, a light saturated page with very round geometry; ours becomes an almost colourless instrument with one saturated dot, at r 12 and hard-edged. Against baby-log (294, cool, chroma 0.10): baby-log is a soft pale lavender that goes very dark at night; ours is a mid-graphite by day with a far more saturated, 24°-distant accent. And against the portfolio's two existing near-achromatic apps — caregiver-log (250, chroma 0.035) and signature-maker (264, chroma 0.022) — both are WARM paper with an EDITORIAL serif voice; ours is cool, technical, and darker. Three axes of separation, not one. (3) CATEGORY. There is no owned colour to avoid the way Adobe owns red in PDF, but there are two traps. Warm pinks and reds are the iLoveIMG/iLovePDF family and also the hue most likely to sit next to skin tones in a preview and bias them — which is why the magenta must be confined to a button and a number, never a background wash. And the bright multicolour gradient is Squoosh's signature; borrowing it would put us in the position of the weaker imitator of the one competitor whose output quality genuinely beats ours. (4) TRUST. In a search result full of anonymous ad-funded clones, a restrained, obviously-built instrument reads as a real product; a colourful friendly one reads as another affiliate page. Practically: keep the skins.mjs row's hue (322 → 318) and voice ('technical', Space Grotesk is right for the numeric readouts), change `chroma` to ~0.02 for the derived surfaces while defining the accent as a separate high-chroma token, change `texture` from 'wash' to 'none', and add a hard-coded `--field:#8c8c8c` that is identical in light and dark mode and is the only permitted background for an image preview.
colorRecommendation.avoid: The current `wash` texture and the pink-white canvas (#fcf5fd) — coloured gradients behind photographs are a functional defect in this app specifically, not a taste question. Any saturated colour touching a preview edge, for the same reason. Warm pink/red as a large surface: it is the iLoveIMG family and it is the worst possible neighbour to skin tones. Squoosh's rainbow gradient — imitating the quality leader's look while shipping weaker encoders is the one positioning we cannot survive. Pure #fff and pure #000 as the field behind images: white makes everything look darker and more contrasty than it is, black does the reverse, and both make a compression judgement unreliable; a fixed mid-grey is the photographic convention and should not flip with the theme. Green as the sole indicator of 'smaller' — the existing support hue 158 is right, but the word 'smaller' and the signed number must carry the meaning too, since red/green is the commonest colour-vision deficiency and this app's core readout is a before/after delta. Animated counters, confetti, or a progress ring that celebrates — completion is an exit, not an event. And do not use the accent decoratively anywhere: at chroma 0.16 on a near-neutral page it will be the loudest thing on screen after the photographs, which is exactly the budget it should spend on the one button that matters.

confidence: MEDIUM-HIGH overall, with a clearly uneven distribution — the parts that will drive the redesign are the strongest, and the parts I would most like to have are missing. HIGHEST CONFIDENCE (read directly from our own repository, not inferred): every single VERIFIED GAP in tableStakes. I read /workspaces/SWS-apps/apps/image-compressor/index.html (1,253 lines), app.js (163), helpers.js (26), sw.js, manifest.webmanifest and README.md. Confirmed by direct inspection: no drag/drop/paste handlers exist anywhere; `downloadStaggered()` fires sequential `<a download>` clicks with a toast asking the user to allow multiple downloads; the only preview is a 120 px data-URL thumbnail of the ORIGINAL and the output is never shown; controls are a five-option maxSide select, a three-option format select and a 30–95 quality range, with no target-size and no typed dimensions; there is no per-row remove and no Clear all; `getContext('2d')` is called with no colorSpace; the PNG path calls toBlob with undefined quality and `savingsPct()` cannot report inflation; the Compress loop is serial, main-thread, with no progress or cancel; `accept="image/*"` plus a bare `createImageBitmap` gives HEIC files the message 'Couldn't read <name>'; and the `.trust` component is defined in CSS but `class="trust"` appears zero times in the markup. Treat all of these as fact. HIGH CONFIDENCE (primary sources fetched directly): Squoosh issue #1259, opened 11 July 2022 and still open, with the quoted batch request and the EXIF/filename/timestamp asks (github.com fetched directly); MDN's statement that `imageOrientation` defaults to `from-image` — which means, importantly, that we most likely do NOT have an EXIF-rotation bug on modern browsers, so I have deliberately not listed one; the FBI Denver file-converter advisory of March 2025 (fbi.gov URL surfaced in search and independently reported by Malwarebytes, BleepingComputer, Help Net Security, Bitdefender and Forbes on 18 March 2025 — I did not fetch fbi.gov itself). MEDIUM CONFIDENCE (secondary but consistent): TinyPNG's 20-image / 5 MB free cap and $39/yr Pro price come from OMR Reviews and NitDit, NOT from the vendor — tinypng.com/pricing 307-redirects to tinify.com/pricing and that URL returned 404 on fetch, so I could not confirm from source. The $25→$39 increase comes from a competitor's marketing blog. TinyPNG's 48-hour retention is a search-result summary of their policy, not a page I read. iLoveIMG's $4/mo-annual / $7/mo-monthly pricing, ~15-files-per-task limit, 2,500 monthly credits and 200 MB ceiling come from saasworthy and from competitors' 'iLoveIMG alternative' pages, several of which are self-serving; I did not fetch iloveimg.com/pricing. Adobe Express's 40 MB limit and JPEG-coercion-on-download come from a competitor blog plus Adobe helpx via search summary. ShortPixel's 100 free credits and ~$9.99 unlimited are from Findstack and review sites. bulkresizephotos' NitroPay ad monetisation is from a search summary of their own privacy policy, not the policy page itself. APP STORE QUOTES — IMPORTANT CAVEAT: apps.apple.com review listings for id1449007043 and id1153379683 were fetched successfully and the reviewer handles, star ratings and dates are as returned, but WebFetch summarises pages through a model, so I cannot guarantee the quoted sentences are character-exact. Treat them as close paraphrase; re-check verbatim before using any of them in public-facing copy. NOT VERIFIED AT ALL, AND THE BIGGEST HOLE: Reddit. WebSearch refuses reddit.com outright ('domains are not accessible to our user agent'), and DuckDuckGo Lite fallbacks returned either nothing or one irrelevant 2014 thread. There is therefore ZERO Reddit evidence in this document, which for a category this consumer-facing is a real gap — someone should manually read r/photography, r/webdev, r/india (the KB-target use case is heavily Indian-portal-driven) and r/iphone before treating the complaint list as complete. Also unverified: Google Play 1–3 star reviews (JS-rendered, unfetchable); G2 and Capterra listings for TinyPNG and ShortPixel; justuseapp's aggregated negative reviews (403). Two claims in the complaints list are explicitly flagged inline as self-serving and should not be quoted publicly: the '200 KB is the Naukri/passport/visa standard' portal thresholds, which come only from the SEO tools' own marketing copy (the DEMAND is well evidenced by the sheer number of pages targeting those queries; the specific portal numbers are not), and the whole 'no upload alternatives' blog cluster, whose value here is as evidence of a crowded claim rather than as a source of facts. Finally, the colour section: the portfolio audit is read directly from /workspaces/SWS-apps/design/skins.mjs and is exact; the perceptual argument about neutral surrounds is well-established colour-science practice and the convention of every professional image tool, but I did not run a user test, and the specific token values proposed (chroma 0.02, accent chroma 0.16, field L 0.55) are a starting point for the build script, not measured values.
